opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think "loss of focus" is a fair description, and I've thought about it a lot. When I look back at my PhD, it doesn't look like one clean line. I worked on edge detection, then network architecture design, then some things around representation learning. From the outside it can look like I was jumping around without a clear thesis.

But I've come to see it differently. At the time, the field itself was changing incredibly fast. Deep learning was just taking off, and the questions worth asking seemed to shift every year. If you held on too tightly to one narrow problem, you could end up polishing something the community had already moved past. So part of the wandering was simply trying to follow where the real questions were going.

There's also a more personal side. As a student, you don't yet know what your taste is. You try things, and some feel right and some don't. I think that exploration is how you figure out what you care about. For me, the common thread turned out to be a fascination with representations: how a model sees the world, and how to build architectures and learning signals that let good representations emerge. I didn't articulate it that way back then. I only recognized it afterward.

So my view now is that focus is often something you discover in hindsight rather than something you plan up front. Having said that, I don't want to romanticize it too much. There were definitely moments when I felt lost and anxious, wondering whether I was building anything coherent. I think that anxiety is pretty normal for a PhD student. What helped was having good collaborators and mentors who reminded me that a career is long, and that one paper or one project doesn't define you.

If I gave advice to students now, I'd say: it's okay to explore, but each time, try to go deep enough to really understand something. Shallow hopping is different from exploration. If you go deep each time, the pieces eventually connect, even if you can't see how while you're in the middle of it.

r001.rationale: The response describes some of the research shifts as exploration and as an effort to follow changing research questions, framing the loss of focus as partly intentional.

r002.rationale: It names representations, architectures, and learning signals as a common thread, but does not identify structural priors guiding deep representation learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "loss of focus" is the wrong framing, even though it's exactly how it felt at the time. During my PhD at UC San Diego, I bounced around a lot. I worked on things that looked like they had nothing to do with each other: edge detection, segmentation, then later the architecture work that became ResNeXt. If you had asked me in year three what my thesis was about, I would have given you a pretty uncomfortable answer.

What I've come to understand is that the wandering was the point. I didn't have a thesis, I had a question I couldn't articulate yet, which was something like: how do you build visual representations that are general, that transfer, that aren't hand-engineered for one task? Every project I did was a partial, clumsy attempt at that question from a different angle. The edge detection work taught me a lot about how low-level structure matters. The architecture work taught me that the inductive biases you bake in determine what the model can and cannot learn. Those lessons only became a coherent story in retrospect.

I think there's a lot of pressure on PhD students to pick a lane early and stay in it. Some people do that very well, and they produce a deep, consistent body of work. But I was never that person, and I spent a lot of energy feeling guilty about it. My advisor Zhuowen Tu was actually quite tolerant of this. He let me explore, which I didn't fully appreciate until later.

The other thing I'd say is that the field itself was shifting under our feet. I started right around the time deep learning was taking over computer vision. So part of what felt like my own lack of focus was actually the whole community re-orienting. The problems I thought I was supposed to work on in 2012 were not the problems that mattered in 2015. Staying loyal to a plan would have meant staying loyal to a world that no longer existed.

So if I'm making sense of it now, I'd say: focus is something you earn, not something you decide. You wander until you find the thing you keep coming back to, and then suddenly it looks like you were focused all along. That's a bit of a convenient story to tell after the fact, I admit. But I think the honest version is that I was curious, I was anxious about being curious, and the curiosity won.

r001.rationale: The response calls the wandering “the point” and describes each project as an attempt at a larger question, framing the apparent loss of focus as partly purposeful exploration.

r002.rationale: It mentions inductive biases in the architecture work, but names the unifying question as building general, transferable visual representations. It does not identify using structural priors to guide deep representation learning as the unifying theme.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d distinguish between exploring different topics and losing focus. During a PhD, you’re still figuring out which questions matter to you, so some exploration is necessary. But there’s a tension: if you move on every time something new looks interesting, you may never stay with a problem long enough to understand it deeply.

The way I make sense of it is to ask whether those projects are helping me develop a clearer set of questions. They don’t all have to fit neatly under one topic. But over time, you want your curiosity to become more deliberate—you want to know why you’re pursuing something, beyond the fact that it’s new.

r001.rationale: It presents exploring different topics during a PhD as necessary while figuring out which questions matter, framing the apparent loss of focus as partly intentional.

r002.rationale: It does not identify structural priors guiding deep representation learning as the unifying theme of Saining Xie’s PhD research.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think there’s a difference between being unfocused and exploring before you know what your focus should be. During a PhD, you’re developing your taste: which problems matter to you, which questions you keep coming back to, and how you like to work. That process doesn’t necessarily look coherent while you’re in it.

Of course, exploration can also become a way to avoid going deep. If you keep switching whenever something gets difficult, that’s a problem. So I’d ask: are these different projects helping you develop a clearer point of view? Can you take something you learned in one direction and use it in another? If so, the apparent loss of focus can be productive. But eventually you have to choose a question and stay with it long enough to contribute something meaningful.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses exploration during a PhD in general, but does not say Saining Xie’s loss of focus was partly intentional.
